newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokyo Nikkei closes at new calendar 1997 high.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo Nikkei closes at new calendar 1997 high.

text.p: The Tokyo stock market's benchmark closed at a new high for calendar year 1997, ending above the 20,500 threshold for the first time since December.
Brokers said strength in stock futures and continued interest in high-technology issues, especially laggards, boosted the index.
The 225-share Nikkei average finished the session at 20,563.16, up 111.31 points or 0.54 percent. It was the highest close since 20,568.38 on December 11.
During the session, the benchmark climbed to a high of 20,671.97, the highest intraday point since the December 11 high of 20,755.74.
Nikkei 225 June futures closed at 20,560, up 120 points.

"Futures were especially firm and so were laggards in the high-technology sector," said Tadahiro Kamogawa, Yamaichi Securities general manager. "But there was also pressure from profit-taking, keeping a tight rein on gains."
Turnover rose to 439 million shares from 311 million on the previous day. Winners beat losers 638 to 437, with 162 issues unchanged.
Fujitsu Ltd topped the list of actively traded issues. The shares rose 20 yen to 1,470, a new high for 1997, on turnover of 8.53 million shares.

"Fujitsu and NEC have started to attract investors as two of the core issues in the high-tech and information network fields," said Seiki Orimi, manager of stock information at Dai-Ichi Securities Co Ltd.
NEC Corp rose 20 yen to 1,650.

Some brokers said the market was also encouraged by news late on Monday that Japan's biggest life insurer, Nippon Life Insurance Co, would accept troubled Nippon Credit Bank Ltd's (NCB) request for aid in increasing its capital.
NCB rose three yen to 250, and was the fourth-most heavily traded issue with turnover of 6.05 million shares.

Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank shares fell as investors were discouraged by a media report that some local governments were cancelling business with the bank due to its suspected loans to racketeers, brokers said. It was the third-largest percentage loser, shedding 70 yen or 4.93 percent to close at 1,350.
The retreating sectors were led by air transport, electric power, iron/steel, retailers and services.

Vague hopes that land liquidity was on the road to recovery and that land prices had bottomed out lifted real estate shares to the top of the list of gaining sectors. They were followed by credit/lease, warehouses, pulp/paper and mining.

"The rise today was due to sound fundamentals," a trader at a middle-sized brokerage said. "There is speculation that pension funds will be allocated in mid-June, and until then the indices are likely to be firm."
Brokers said they were also keeping an eye on Sony Corp shares, which closed at a new record high of 10,100 yen, up 160.

"Investors believe that stocks are likely to be firm in the coming sessions, but there are some doubts about the momentum," a broker at a second-tier brokerage said. "If Sony finds a firm footing over 10,000 yen, it will improve market sentiment greatly."
Market sources said that after the Nikkei average digests the profit-taking wall looming between 20,500 and 21,000, it could eventually try for 22,000.
In other indices, the TOPIX added 4.10 points or 0.27 percent to end at 1,511.93. The Nikkei 300 rose 0.54 point or 0.19 percent to finish at 291.91.
The second section index rose 2.31 points or 0.13 percent to end at 1,788.63. Second section turnover was 10.35 million shares, up from 7.61 million in the previous session.
The over-the-counter index was up 1.32 points or 0.11 percent at 1,187.72 in late Tokyo afternoon.
--Masako Iijima, Tokyo Equities Desk (+81-3-3432-9052)
